title: Logs (south)
description: Every log source the management plane ships: host journals, PostgreSQL's own log, and container logs for a chosen set of namespaces. Built because the AWX outage on 2026-08-23 was diagnosed from a file over SSH and from `kubectl logs`, which retained eight minutes.

list.name: instance
list.label: host
list.description: Falls back to .* so the panels below still work if the label query returns nothing -- an empty variable would silently match no streams and read as a quiet estate.

panels.title: Lines per source
panels.description: A source going flat is as interesting as one spiking. journald is always the loudest; postgresql is normally near-silent, so sustained volume there means something is being logged repeatedly.

panels.title: Errors in range
panels.description: journald error/crit/alert/emerg plus PostgreSQL FATAL/ERROR/PANIC. Not a health score: a quiet estate and a dead collector both read zero. Cross-check against 'Lines per source' being non-zero.

panels.title: PostgreSQL — FATAL, ERROR, PANIC
panels.description: The panel that would have ended the 2026-08-23 incident in one look. 'remaining connection slots are reserved' appeared here 1,280 times from 10:28 UTC while every dashboard stayed green, because this log goes to a file and nothing was collecting it.

panels.title: Kernel trouble — lockups, OOM kills, hung tasks
panels.description: The query the 2026-08-22 lockup investigation needed and did not have. dmesg wraps and a reboot erases it; this survives 14 days. A soft lockup here is the evidence that rung 3 of the escalation ladder is the right rung.

targets.expr: {job="journal", instance=~"$instance"} |~ "(?i)watchdog|soft lockup|hard lockup|oom-kill|out of memory|blocked for more than"

panels.title: AWX containers — errors and tracebacks
panels.description: AWX is the hands: every verb in infra-objectives runs through it. Its pod logs previously lived only in the container's own 8-minute window.

panels.title: Container log volume by namespace
panels.description: Watch this against the 50GB/month allowance. Namespaces are an allow-list in roles/alloy defaults; cert-manager and nginx-ingress are deliberately excluded.

panels.title: Journal volume by unit (top talkers)
panels.description: Useful for spotting a unit that has started shouting. A sudden new talker is often the first sign of something retrying.

panels.title: What is and is not collected

options.content:
**Collected:** the systemd journal from all four hosts (including `kubelet` and `containerd`); PostgreSQL's own log; container logs for `awx`, `kube-system` and `kube-flannel`.

**Not collected, deliberately:** `cert-manager` and `nginx-ingress` container logs (owner's call), and `doppler-operator-system`. Adding one is an entry in `alloy_pod_log_namespaces`, not a code change — but check the volume first: the current selection is about 13 MB/day against a 50GB/month allowance.

**Retention is 14 days.** For anything older the run ledgers in `infra-objectives/state/` are the record, and they are the only durable account — AWX prunes its own job history too.

**Two traps this pipeline already hit, worth knowing when reading it back:**

- **PostgreSQL's log is a file, not journald.** `logging_collector=off` with `log_destination=stderr` lands in `/var/log/postgresql/`. A journald-only collector sees the unit start and stop and nothing else — so during the 2026-08-23 incident a Loki search for the refusals returned empty while 1,280 of them sat on disk. An empty result was a blind check, not health.
- **Timestamps are the log's own, not the collection time.** That needed an explicit `stage.timestamp`; without it the first backfill stamped an entire day's history — refusals from 10:28, a restart at 17:39 — as all having happened at 18:40:08. An incident timeline that is confidently wrong is worse than a missing one.

**Absence of logs is not evidence of health.** If a source goes flat, check `Lines per source` before concluding anything: a dead collector and a quiet host look identical from here, which is why the dead-man's switch is a separate concern.
